questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y) & =2{x}^{2}y+1 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =1 \\ g(y) & =y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+y+C.
$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4-2xy
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}-x{y}^{2}+g(y)\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2xy+{g}^{′}(y).

$$
\begin{aligned}-2xy+{g}^{′}(y) & =4-2xy \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =4 \\ g(y) & =4y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=4y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}-x{y}^{2}+4y+C.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+(3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z})\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+C.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=-y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2yz & =-2yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{z}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{z}-2z & =xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{z}+{x}^{2}+y-{z}^{2}+C.
$$
